title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: who did it, who is blamed, what the notice really says

questions.prompt: Nobody asked Hedi to do it and no teacher suggested it: he decided on his own that he would learn forty new words a week, and he wrote that figure at the top of his revision plan. Which sentence reports that in correct English?

options.text: Hedi set himself a target of forty words a week.
Hedi set him a target of forty words a week.
Hedi set his self a target of forty words a week.
Hedi set to himself a target of forty words a week.

questions.explanation: "Hedi set himself a target of forty words a week." is right: the person who fixes the figure and the person who has to reach it are one and the same, and the reflexive is what English puts in that place, straight after the verb. "Hedi set him a target of forty words a week." is perfectly correct English, but it tells a different story: an object pronoun always points away from the subject, so the figure would have been fixed for somebody else, when the situation says that Hedi fixed it for his own use. "Hedi set his self a target of forty words a week." splits a word that English writes in one piece; there is himself, and there is no his self. And "Hedi set to himself a target of forty words a week." adds a preposition the pattern refuses: you set somebody a target, or you set a target for somebody, so set a target for himself would have been another correct way of saying it, but never set to himself.

questions.prompt: The results have just been posted and four pupils are talking in the corridor. All four sentences below are built on should have or shouldn't have plus a past participle. Which one expresses a regret about the speaker's own choice, and not a reproach aimed at somebody else?

options.text: You shouldn't have left the last page blank.
You should have asked the teacher for the reading list.
Hedi should have started his revision much earlier.
I should have checked my answers before the bell.

questions.explanation: "I should have checked my answers before the bell." is the regret: the form says that a sensible action was not carried out, and because the subject is the speaker, what comes out is regret and not blame. "You shouldn't have left the last page blank." uses the same structure, but the subject is the person spoken to, so the sentence blames that person for something already done, which is a reproach. "You should have asked the teacher for the reading list." is a reproach too, this time for an action that was never carried out at all. And "Hedi should have started his revision much earlier." moves the blame onto a third person who is named, which changes nothing to the value: the speaker is judging somebody else, not looking back on a paper of their own.

questions.prompt: A form teacher says four things to the same pupil in the course of one morning. One of them is a warning: it announces something unpleasant that will follow at once if the pupil does not act. Which sentence is the warning?

options.text: You ought to give a hand to the pupils who joined the class in January.
You had better learn that list tonight; the test is tomorrow.
You needn't copy out the whole text; the first paragraph is enough.
You should read a page of English every evening.

questions.explanation: "You had better learn that list tonight; the test is tomorrow." is the warning: had better always has a bad result standing behind it, and here the sentence names that result itself, since the paper comes the next morning and the words will not be there. "You ought to give a hand to the pupils who joined the class in January." states a duty, what a decent classmate does, and nothing unpleasant is announced if the pupil does nothing. "You needn't copy out the whole text; the first paragraph is enough." does the opposite of warning: it lifts an effort the pupil believed compulsory. And "You should read a page of English every evening." is ordinary advice about a habit, with no deadline over it and no consequence attached.

questions.prompt: Rania's brother says four things to her in the week before her exams. One tells her that an effort is unnecessary, one says what he works out from what he can see, one blames her for something she did not do, and one offers to do a piece of the work himself. Which sentence is the offer?

options.text: Your last page is full of crossings out: you must have been rushing.
You needn't learn the dates by heart; they are printed on the paper.
I can go over the irregular verbs with you after supper.
You should have asked for the reading list back in September.

questions.explanation: "I can go over the irregular verbs with you after supper." is the offer: the work falls on the speaker, the good of it goes to the person he is speaking to, and can here is neither a request nor a boast about what he is able to do. "Your last page is full of crossings out: you must have been rushing." orders nothing at all: he is concluding from what lies in front of him, which is a deduction, and must have plus a past participle is how English draws that conclusion about something already over. "You needn't learn the dates by heart; they are printed on the paper." lifts an effort she believed compulsory, so it frees her, but it hands her no help. And "You should have asked for the reading list back in September." turns should have on somebody else and blames her for a sensible thing she never did, which is a reproach.

questions.prompt: Read this paragraph, written by a pupil for the school magazine, then answer. "(1) Banning phones for the whole school day is a heavier rule than the staff room admits. (2) Nobody denies that a class works better when no screen lights up in the third row. (3) Yet a pupil who travels forty minutes each way has one safe means of reaching home, and the ban takes it away. (4) The rule should stop at the classroom door, not at the school gate." Which sentence is the point the writer concedes to the other side?

options.text: Sentence 2, because it grants the other side a real advantage.
Sentence 1, because it opens by rejecting the rule outright.
Sentence 3, because it is introduced by the linker Yet.
Sentence 4, because it states what the whole paragraph is aiming at.

questions.explanation: "Sentence 2, because it grants the other side a real advantage." is right: a concession is the one sentence in which a writer admits that the people he is arguing against have a fair point, and Nobody denies that is one of the expressions English keeps for that move. "Sentence 1, because it opens by rejecting the rule outright." describes the thesis, the position the writer defends from the first line, which is the opposite of a concession. "Sentence 3, because it is introduced by the linker Yet." mistakes the answer for the admission: Yet marks the return to the writer's own argument, and it can only come after a concession. And "Sentence 4, because it states what the whole paragraph is aiming at." names the conclusion, which by definition follows the writer's side and never the other one.

questions.prompt: Rania has written this line on her vocabulary card: "to distinguish = to be exactly like the others". Her definition belongs to another verb of the theme. Which of these four gives the real meaning of the verb she wrote?

options.text: to do what the rest of the group does, exactly as the rules ask
to tell one thing apart from another, or to set it apart
to stop something from being seen or heard any longer
to go over a finished paper once more, hunting for slips

questions.explanation: "to tell one thing apart from another, or to set it apart" is the meaning of distinguish, and it works in both directions: you distinguish one twin from the other when you can tell which is which, and a badge distinguishes a school from its neighbours when it sets the two apart for everybody to see. "to do what the rest of the group does, exactly as the rules ask" is the meaning of conform to, and it is in fact what Rania wrote on her card, which is how the two verbs got exchanged: they pull in opposite directions. "to stop something from being seen or heard any longer" is suppress, the verb the uniform lesson uses of a school accused of hiding what makes each pupil different. And "to go over a finished paper once more, hunting for slips" is check, which belongs to the exam lesson and has nothing to do with telling two things apart.
